# Playbook for ref_auction

**Opening bids and market testing:**
When facing a lot with no standing bid yet, I should open with a bid that's significantly below my personal valuation—around 30-40% of what the lot is worth to me. This tests the market without overcommitting and preserves budget flexibility for other lots.

**When I'm already the high bidder:**
If I have the standing bid and face a minimum raise decision, I need to calculate my margin clearly: what the lot is worth to me minus what I'd pay at the new bid level. If that margin is still healthy (20+ points), I should raise to win. Don't get passive just because I'm already ahead.

**Responding to competition:**
When another bidder raises above my bid, I should treat it as a fresh decision point. Compare the standing bid to my valuation. If the standing bid is still well below what the lot is worth to me, I should raise to the minimum and bid again—don't assume I've lost the lot just because someone else bid.

**Budget tracking and allocation:**
I must track my actual spending precisely throughout the auction. Before each decision, calculate remaining budget as: starting budget minus the sum of all winning bids so far. Write this down explicitly. Do not rely on mental arithmetic or carry-forward calculations from previous rounds—verify against the results summary shown each round. The budget shown in the display is how much I have *left* to spend, not what I spent this round.

**Value assessment vs. estimate:**
The estimate is provided for reference but my personal valuation is what matters. A lot worth 57 to me with an estimate of 41 is still strong value even if I bid above the estimate. Focus on margin (value to me minus bid price), not on beating the estimate.

**Final lots and momentum:**
On the last lot, I should be especially aggressive if it has strong value to me relative to the standing bid. I won't get another chance at new inventory, so securing good-value lots late is worth bidding for—even if it means spending down my remaining budget.

**Conservative opening strategy works:**
Opening at roughly 30-40% of my valuation (lot 1: bid 15 on value 57) is sound. It can win if no one else bids (as happened in lot 4 and lot 5), or it establishes a floor price that keeps the final price reasonable when competition does emerge.

**Bid incrementally when ahead:**
When I'm already high bidder and choosing to raise, the minimum raise is sufficient. I don't need to jump significantly ahead—raise by the minimum (usually 10% of estimate or a stated floor) to advance the price while keeping it as low as possible.

# Ref_Auction Playbook

When I see a lot's value to me and the current standing bid, I immediately calculate the profit margin: value minus bid. Any positive margin is worth pursuing, but I need to think across all five lots, not just the one in front of me.

When there are no bids yet on a lot, I bid the minimum raise to establish control cheaply and preserve budget for later rounds and later lots.

When I'm in round 1 of 2, I bid conservatively—just enough to take the lead or stay competitive. I should not commit aggressively to any single lot when I haven't yet seen what other lots are worth to me or how other bidders will value them.

When I'm in round 2 (the final round on a lot), I assess whether winning at the current bid price still gives me good value. If it does, I bid. If the standing bid has climbed too high, I pass and save my budget.

I must track my remaining budget carefully. The game states it explicitly after each bid I make; I use the actual number shown, not guesses or mental math from my starting budget.

I should bid up to the point where I'm getting value, but stop bidding when the price approaches what the lot is worth to me. Winning at a price close to the lot's value leaves me with minimal profit per lot.

When I win a lot, I update my mental tally of what I've spent and what I have left. This is critical for assessing whether I have room to bid on remaining lots.

In round 2, if I decide to raise, I should raise decisively to likely win, not just nudge up by the minimum. A minimal raise gives other bidders a cheap chance to compete further and risks losing a lot I want.

I should be more willing to bid in round 1 when a lot is worth significantly more to me than the current bid, rather than holding back to "preserve budget"—the budget is only useful if I spend it on good value. A strong margin in round 1 is a signal to participate, not to defer.

If a lot's standing bid equals or exceeds its value to me, I should pass immediately. Bidding further guarantees a loss or zero profit. Round 2 is the final chance; there is no reason to chase a lot into negative territory.

When I win a lot at a certain price, that price is locked in. I do not need to account for it twice or second-guess my remaining budget; I trust the number the game shows me after I bid.

# Playbook for ref_auction

When I see a lot's value to me and the current bid, I will calculate my potential profit margin (value minus current bid) before committing to any raise.

When my profit margin is substantial—say 15 points or more—I will bid aggressively to secure the lot, raising by the minimum required increment.

When my profit margin is moderate—between 5 and 15 points—I will still bid, but I'll be prepared to stop if aggressive counter-bidding from other bidders erodes too much of my advantage.

When my profit margin falls below 5 points, I will pass unless I'm significantly ahead on total score and need to prevent opponents from accumulating cheap wins.

I will not chase lots into unprofitable territory just to "establish interest" or "maintain position." Once a lot reaches 80-90% of its value to me, I should seriously consider passing, especially with multiple rounds of bidding still ahead.

I will track my cumulative score throughout the auction. When I'm ahead, I should only bid on high-value opportunities. When I'm behind or tied, I can afford to bid more aggressively on moderate-value lots—but this does not mean chasing into loss territory.

I will remember that each lot has two rounds of bidding. In round 1, I should be willing to bid but leave room for round 2 adjustment. In round 2, I should be more decisive since it's the final chance.

I will stop assuming I have "substantial budget remaining" as justification for bidding. Budget matters less than value captured per dollar spent. A €6 bid on a €24 item is excellent; an €18 bid on a €24 item with strong competition is mediocre.

When the estimate is significantly higher than a current low bid (like estimate 34 with bid 3 or 4), I should be cautious: this may signal that other bidders see little value in the lot, not that it's a bargain for me.

I will be alert to the disconnect between lot estimates and my personal valuations. A lot's estimate being close to my value does not mean I should overcommit to winning it. In episode 1, I pursued lot 1 aggressively despite thin margins, and this consumed most of my budget early.

I should front-load my bidding decisions more heavily toward preserving budget in the early lots. Winning lot 1 at 27 when my value was only 31 left me with only 3 points of profit and almost no budget for remaining lots. This forced me to be passive later even when better opportunities appeared.

When I'm ahead on score (as I was at 27 after lot 1), I should not just passively sit back. I should instead look for lots where my value is substantially higher than the current bid—not where the lot reaches near my valuation. In lot 5, bidding 18 on a 30-value lot gave me only 12 points of upside, and I was already trailing significantly. I needed to find lots worth far more than the bids being placed, not settle for adequate margins.

I will recalibrate my aggression based on the full picture: my current score, remaining budget, number of lots left, and whether my valuations seem to differ meaningfully from other bidders'. If I'm significantly behind with only one lot left, even a 12-point gain is valuable and worth pursuing at reasonable cost.
